rounds.fact: Juno offered free dial-up internet paid for entirely by advertising, and later merged with rival NetZero to survive the end of the free-ISP era.
USA Today's website carried over the newspaper's signature colorful infographics and short-story format, designed for readers scanning quickly rather than reading in depth.
LimeWire became one of the most popular peer-to-peer file-sharing programs after Napster's shutdown, before being forced offline itself by a 2010 court injunction.
The New York Times went online in 1996 and required free registration from the start, a controversial-at-the-time model that foreshadowed the paywalls most news sites use today.
Tripod was a major free website-builder alongside GeoCities and Angelfire, and was eventually bought by Lycos as part of its portal strategy in the late 90s.
